analysis.one_liner: Makes online marketplaces liable when sellers use them to hawk counterfeit health-and-safety goods, unless the marketplace screens listings.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to crack down on counterfeit goods sold online never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from May 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The SHOP SAFE Act would make e-commerce platforms legally liable when a third-party seller uses a counterfeit trademark to sell goods that can hurt people — fake medicines, electronics, toys, or auto parts. A platform can escape that liability only by verifying each seller's identity and U.S. contact for lawsuits, prescreening listings with technology, showing the country of origin, banning repeat counterfeiters, and taking a list of other preventive steps at its own expense. The idea is to put the cost of stopping dangerous fakes on the marketplaces that profit from third-party sales, rather than leaving it to shoppers and the brands whose trademarks get stolen.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers buying health- and safety-related products online, who would face fewer dangerous counterfeits; and trademark-owning brands, who would gain a powerful new way to force platforms to police counterfeits on their behalf. Small platforms under $500,000 in annual sales are exempt until they rack up ten infringement notices.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms would be presumed liable for a seller's use of a counterfeit mark on goods that can cause illness, injury, or death, unless the platform took preventive steps first.

To escape liability, a platform must verify sellers' identities and U.S. registered agents, prescreen listings with technology at no cost to brand owners, display each listing's country of origin and manufacture, remove suspicious listings promptly, and terminate sellers who use counterfeit marks in three separate listings within a year.
Platforms must show verified seller information and the country goods ship from, so buyers can judge what they are purchasing, though personal home addresses must be shielded.

analysis.who_pays: Large e-commerce platforms would bear the cost of building and running seller-verification and screening systems, and would face lawsuits if dangerous counterfeits slip through. Small and foreign third-party sellers would face new hurdles — a U.S. registered agent or verified service address, identity verification, and contractual agreements — which could raise selling costs or push some small sellers off platforms entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online marketplaces and small third-party sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill makes screening and removal technology the platform's obligation at no cost to brand owners, so compliance costs would fall on marketplaces and likely be passed down to sellers and shoppers as higher fees.

Requiring every seller to designate a U.S. registered agent or verified service address would be a real burden for small and overseas sellers, and the text adds no funding or safe harbor to help them comply.

The definition of a platform is broad — any electronically accessed service that lets others sell physical goods to U.S. consumers — so communities, classified sites, and niche marketplaces with modest sales could be pulled in after just ten infringement notices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-safety benefit is genuine: counterfeit medicines, chargers, and children's products cause real injuries, and today platforms generally face no trademark liability for what third parties sell. But the bill works almost entirely by shifting enforcement duty and cost onto marketplaces, with the burden landing hardest on small sellers who did nothing wrong, and it gives brand owners a leverage tool that goes well beyond the dangerous-goods problem it is pitched on. It is a defensible trade — platforms profit from third-party sales and are positioned to screen — but the design is one-sided and the exemption threshold is arbitrary.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2021 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee in November 2022, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023 without ever getting a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on May 20, 2021 with three original cosponsors — Reps. Issa (R-CA), Johnson (D-GA), and Cline (R-VA) — making the introduction bipartisan.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
On November 1, 2022, near the end of the Congress, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet — a step short of any committee vote.
No further action was taken, and the bill expired with the 117th Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online marketplaces avoided a new strict-liability regime and its compliance costs, and sellers of counterfeits continued operating under the weaker notice-and-takedown status quo, while shoppers kept bearing the risk of dangerous fakes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Marketplaces and counterfeit sellers, not shoppers

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee.

for.name: Reps. Issa (R-CA), Johnson (D-GA), and Cline (R-VA)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup in the 19 months the bill sat in committee; its only movement was a late referral to a subcommittee in November 2022.

against.name: Online marketplace operators and small-seller groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly objected to strict platform liability and seller-verification mandates like those in SHOP SAFE, warning of costs to marketplaces and barriers for small and overseas sellers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four original sponsors split evenly between two Democrats and two Republicans, and no recorded opposition ever emerged in committee; the bill died of inaction rather than a party-line vote.

industries.note: Marketplaces with $500,000 or more in annual sales would face presumed liability for counterfeit health-and-safety goods unless they built verification and screening systems at their own expense. Their interest in the bill was to avoid that liability and cost, which would have left shoppers exposed to dangerous fakes.

Brands would gain a new cause of action to force platforms to police counterfeits on their behalf, with the platforms footing the bill for screening. Their interest in sweeping out counterfeits runs alongside consumers' interest in not buying fake medicines or unsafe products.

Sellers would need a U.S. registered agent or verified service address, verified identity, and signed anti-counterfeiting agreements before selling. Some of that burden genuinely protects buyers, but the cost and paperwork would fall hardest on small sellers who sell legitimate goods.
